concept.name: Volatility skew
concept.definition: Volatility skew is the asymmetric form of the volatility smile in which implied volatility decreases monotonically as strike rises — out-of-the-money puts trading at richer implied volatilities than at-the-money and out-of-the-money calls. It is the persistent pattern in equity and equity-index options, reflecting demand for downside protection and the market's pricing of negative return skewness.
concept.intuition: Equity traders pay up for crash insurance and sell upside lottery tickets cheap, so implied volatility tilts: expensive on the low strikes, cheap on the high strikes.
concept.mechanics: Skew is measured as the slope of implied volatility across strikes or deltas for a fixed expiry, and is quoted in volatility markets via risk reversals (IV of a delta call minus the matching put). Structural drivers include institutional put hedging ('investment skew') and concentrated speculative demand ('demand skew'); skew steepens in sell-offs and flattens in calm rallies.
concept.formula: Skew quote: RR(25d) = IV(25-delta call) - IV(25-delta put); a negative value indicates downside puts richer than upside calls.
concept.failure_modes: Trading the skew as if it were a stable statistical object fails in regime shifts — skew flattens violently during squeezes and steepens in crashes, hurting positions calibrated to historical averages. Cross-sectional skew comparisons also break down when term structures differ.
concept.misconceptions: Steep skew does not mean a crash is imminent: it is a chronic feature of equity option pricing since 1987, reflecting hedging demand and risk premia rather than a point forecast. Nor does rich put skew automatically make put buying a bad trade — it must be weighed against realized crash frequency.
concept.example: A 30-day SPX 25-delta risk reversal of -4 vol points means the 25-delta put trades 4 implied-volatility points above the 25-delta call, the market's standard pricing of downside asymmetry.
